messages.body_plain:
Oh, thanks for the clarification. Can you recommend any resources for me to learn more about censoring processes in missingness models?

On Thu, 26 Aug 2021 at 9:48 pm, 'Pat Malone' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> Unfortunately, that  sensitivity analysis will only distinguish between MCAR and MAR.
>
> Your missingness model may need to include a censoring process, but if you're doing a full missingness strategy for MNAR, that shouldn't be much of an extra issue.
>
> On Thu, Aug 26, 2021 at 7:34 AM Atanas Janackovski <atanas.ja...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thank you Pat. I've been looking at some approaches using the mice package  under MNAR, but I will look into these too.
> >
> > I've started a sensitivity analysis by dropping the observations with missing data and the pattern of results so far is similar.
> >
> > I'm glad that an RI-CLPM will be usable because I think this approach suits the aims of the study. But is it still okay that I only stop at 5 waves, even for those have more sessions?
> >
> > Thanks again.
> >
> > On Thu, 26 Aug 2021 at 9:23 pm, 'Pat Malone' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > > Atanas,
> > >
> > > The fact that you're using RI-CLPM isn't a problem. It just means that some of the simpler solutions to your missingness problem won't be helpful. I don't  have specific suggestions for techniques to model the non-random missing with your SEM, but you might try the work of Craig Enders or Karthika Mohan (e.g., https://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r448-reprint.pdf looks like it might be helpful, but I haven't read it closely).
> > >
> > > Good luck!
> > >
> > > P.S. I was Dorian Lamis's doctoral mentor :)
> > >
> > > On Wed, Aug 25, 2021 at 7:29 PM Atanas Janackovski <atanas.ja...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Thank you Pat.
> > > >
> > > > So, the research question is related to testing the Interpersonal Psychological Theory of Suicide (IPTS) in a non-experimental clinical sample. See picture of purported path model below. The theory states that four factors: perceived burdensomeness, thwarted belongingness, hopelessness and acquired capability are necessary and required to lead to suicide. It also states, that address thwarted belongingness or perceived burdensomeness will lead to reductions in suicidal desire. However, depression is also commonly associated with suicidality.
> > > >
> > > > Most the research has been cross-sectional in nature, even the ones that include more than one time point (including some I have been involved in). The models that have tested this before are mediated regression that used change scores to predicted change in suicidality. However, the underlying assumption to this type of "outcome" research, is that indeed the factors posited by the IPTS do indeed lead to suicidality. But, as most research is cross-sectional in nature, it has not looked at time-to-time changes in these factors. One recent study has used the RI-CLPM to ask this question, using beginning, mid and end point data from an RCT clinical intervention (Abbott, et. al., 2021). They found that the theory doesn't hold, that is, that changes in the theoretical variables don't predict changes in suicidality.
> > > >
> > > > Regarding missing data, data for some participants is MNAR, because they have completed therapy after 2, 3, … n, sessions. For others, they will continue beyond the 5 waves that I am wanting to test (but may have missing data between sessions 2–4 for other reasons, although there is not too much missing in this regard, apart from one questionnaire not being complete, for example). I have the total sessions each person attended over their episode of therapy and was entering this as covariate loading onto the random intercepts (as well as age, sex, and acquired capability as baseline [as it was only measured once in the sample, and is theoretically consistent to only measure once as it is more 'trait' like]).
> > > >
> > > > So, given this, is there any reason that I cannot use a RI-CLPM? If it is related to MNAR, what is the approach to this? Multiple imputation? Or is the design not able to be carried out at all?
> > > >
> > > > I'm not sure if it is helpful or not, but have posted my code below just in case…
> > > >
> > > > Thanks again for your help, and please let me know if you need any more information about by questions.
> > > >
> > > > Interpersonal Psychological Theory of Suicide
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > (Van Orden, et. al, 2010)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Model specification
> > > >
> > > > This was developed with the help of the Mulder and Hamaker (2020) article and example code.
> > > >
> > > > riclpm_byc_si_cov <- '
> > > >   ## Create between components (random intercepts)
> > > >   RIpb  =~ 1*pb_1 + 1*pb_2 + 1*pb_3 + 1*pb_4 + 1*pb_5
> > > >   RItb  =~ 1*tb_1 + 1*tb_2 + 1*tb_3 + 1*tb_4 + 1*tb_5
> > > >   RIbhs =~ 1*bhs_1 + 1*bhs_2 + 1*bhs_3 + 1*bhs_4 + 1*bhs_5
> > > >   RIdep =~ 1*dep_1 + 1*dep_2 + 1*dep_3 + 1*dep_4 + 1*dep_5
> > > >   RIsi  =~ 1*si_1 + 1*si_2 + 1*si_3 + 1*si_4 + 1*si_5
> > > >   ## Create within-person centered variables
> > > >   wpb_1 =~ 1*pb_1
> > > >   wpb_2 =~ 1*pb_2
> > > >   wpb_3 =~ 1*pb_3
> > > >   wpb_4 =~ 1*pb_4
> > > >   wpb_5 =~ 1*pb_5
> > > >   ## ==
> > > >   wtb_1 =~ 1*tb_1
> > > >   wtb_2 =~ 1*tb_2
> > > >   wtb_3 =~ 1*tb_3
> > > >   wtb_4 =~ 1*tb_4
> > > >   wtb_5 =~ 1*tb_5
> > > >   ## ==
> > > >   wbhs_1 =~ 1*bhs_1
> > > >   wbhs_2 =~ 1*bhs_2
> > > >   wbhs_3 =~ 1*bhs_3
> > > >   wbhs_4 =~ 1*bhs_4
> > > >   wbhs_5 =~ 1*bhs_5
> > > >   ## ==
> > > >   wdep_1 =~ 1*dep_1
> > > >   wdep_2 =~ 1*dep_2
> > > >   wdep_3 =~ 1*dep_3
> > > >   wdep_4 =~ 1*dep_4
> > > >   wdep_5 =~ 1*dep_5
> > > >   ## ==
> > > >   wsi_1 =~ 1*si_1
> > > >   wsi_2 =~ 1*si_2
> > > >   wsi_3 =~ 1*si_3
> > > >   wsi_4 =~ 1*si_4
> > > >   wsi_5 =~ 1*si_5
> > > >   ##
> > > >   ## =======
> > > >   ## covariates
> > > >   ## =======
> > > >   ## Regression of random intercepts on covariates.
> > > >   ## -------
> > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ ac_1 # Constrained over time.
> > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ age
> > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ sex_mf
> > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ cov_sess
> > > >   ## =====
> > > >   ##
> > > >   ## Estimate the lagged effects between the within-person centered variables.
> > > >   wpb_2 + wtb_2 + wbhs_2 + wdep_2 + wsi_2 ~ wpb_1 + wtb_1 + wbhs_1 + wdep_1 + wsi_1
> > > >   wpb_3 + wtb_3 + wbhs_3 + wdep_3 + wsi_3 ~ wpb_2 + wtb_2 + wbhs_2 + wdep_2 + wsi_2
> > > >   wpb_4 + wtb_4 + wbhs_4 + wdep_4 + wsi_4 ~ wpb_3 + wtb_3 + wbhs_3 + wdep_3 + wsi_3
> > > >   wpb_5 + wtb_5 + wbhs_5 + wdep_5 + wsi_5 ~ wpb_4 + wtb_4 + wbhs_4 + wdep_4 + wsi_4
> > > >   ## ==
> > > >   ## Estimate the covariance between the within-person centered variables
> > > >   ## at the first wave.
> > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wtb_1 # Covariance
> > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wbhs_1
> > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wdep_1
> > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wsi_1
> > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wbhs_1
> > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wdep_1
> > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wsi_1
> > > >   wbhs_1 ~~ wsi_1
> > > >   wbhs_1 ~~ wdep_1
> > > >   wdep_1 ~~ wsi_1
> > > >   ## Estimate the covariances between the residuals of the within-person
> > > >   ## centered variables (the innovations).
> > > >   ## time_2
> > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wtb_2
> > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wbhs_2
> > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wdep_2
> > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wsi_2
> > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wbhs_2
> > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wdep_2
> > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wsi_2
> > > >   wbhs_2 ~~ wsi_2
> > > >   wbhs_2 ~~ wdep_2
> > > >   wdep_2 ~~ wsi_2
> > > >   ## time_3
> > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wtb_3
> > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wbhs_3
> > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wdep_3
> > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wsi_3
> > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wbhs_3
> > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wdep_3
> > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wsi_3
> > > >   wbhs_3 ~~ wsi_3
> > > >   wbhs_3 ~~ wdep_3
> > > >   wdep_3 ~~ wsi_3
> > > >   ## time_4
> > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wtb_4
> > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wbhs_4
> > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wdep_4
> > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wsi_4
> > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wbhs_4
> > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wdep_4
> > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wsi_4
> > > >   wbhs_4 ~~ wsi_4
> > > >   wbhs_4 ~~ wdep_4
> > > >   wdep_4 ~~ wsi_4
> > > >   ## time_5
> > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wtb_5
> > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wbhs_5
> > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wdep_5
> > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wsi_5
> > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wbhs_5
> > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wdep_5
> > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wsi_5
> > > >   wbhs_5 ~~ wsi_5
> > > >   wbhs_5 ~~ wdep_5
> > > >   wdep_5 ~~ wsi_5
> > > >   ## Estimate the variance and covariance of the random intercepts.
> > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIpb
> > > >   RItb  ~~ RItb
> > > >   RIbhs ~~ RIbhs
> > > >   RIdep ~~ RIdep
> > > >   RIsi  ~~ RIsi
> > > >   ## ==
> > > >   RIpb  ~~ RItb
> > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIbhs
> > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIdep
> > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIsi
> > > >   RItb  ~~ RIbhs
> > > >   RItb  ~~ RIdep
> > > >   RItb  ~~ RIsi
> > > >   RIbhs ~~ RIsi
> > > >   RIbhs ~~ RIdep
> > > >   RIdep ~~ RIsi
> > > >   ## Estimate the (residual) variance of the within-person centered variables.
> > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wpb_1 # Variances
> > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wtb_1
> > > >   wbhs_1 ~~ wbhs_1
> > > >   wdep_1 ~~ wdep_1
> > > >   wsi_1  ~~ wsi_1
> > > >   ## time_2
> > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wpb_2 # Residual variances
> > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wtb_2
> > > >   wbhs_2 ~~ wbhs_2
> > > >   wdep_2 ~~ wdep_2
> > > >   wsi_2  ~~ wsi_2
> > > >   ## time_3
> > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wpb_3 # Residual variances
> > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wtb_3
> > > >   wbhs_3 ~~ wbhs_3
> > > >   wdep_3 ~~ wdep_3
> > > >   wsi_3  ~~ wsi_3
> > > >   ## time_4
> > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wpb_4 # Residual variances
> > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wtb_4
> > > >   wbhs_4 ~~ wbhs_4
> > > >   wdep_4 ~~ wdep_4
> > > >   wsi_4  ~~ wsi_4
> > > >   ## time_5
> > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wpb_5 # Residual variances
> > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wtb_5
> > > >   wbhs_5 ~~ wbhs_5
> > > >   wdep_5 ~~ wdep_5
> > > >   wsi_5  ~~ wsi_5

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > My question is, can I actually use this type of analysis with this data set? Are there any assumptions I am violating by specifying the model this way?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I have searched the internet as well as looked for primary sources, however I cannot seem to find anything to help me. Please let me know if you need more information about my questions.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thanks in advance.

messages.body_plain:
I would look at the general methods for MNAR. We're getting beyond my expertise.

On Thu, Aug 26, 2021 at 7:56 AM Atanas Janackovski <atanas.ja...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Oh, thanks for the clarification. Can you recommend any resources for me to learn more about censoring processes in missingness models?
>
>
> On Thu, 26 Aug 2021 at 9:48 pm, 'Pat Malone' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > Unfortunately, that  sensitivity analysis will only distinguish between MCAR and MAR.
> >
> > Your missingness model may need to include a censoring process, but if you're doing a full missingness strategy for MNAR, that shouldn't be much of an extra issue.
> >
> > On Thu, Aug 26, 2021 at 7:34 AM Atanas Janackovski <atanas.ja...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Thank you Pat. I've been looking at some approaches using the mice package  under MNAR, but I will look into these too.
> > >
> > > I've started a sensitivity analysis by dropping the observations with missing data and the pattern of results so far is similar.
> > >
> > > I'm glad that an RI-CLPM will be usable because I think this approach suits the aims of the study. But is it still okay that I only stop at 5 waves, even for those have more sessions?
> > >
> > > Thanks again.
> > >
> > > On Thu, 26 Aug 2021 at 9:23 pm, 'Pat Malone' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > > > Atanas,
> > > >
> > > > The fact that you're using RI-CLPM isn't a problem. It just means that some of the simpler solutions to your missingness problem won't be helpful. I don't  have specific suggestions for techniques to model the non-random missing with your SEM, but you might try the work of Craig Enders or Karthika Mohan (e.g., https://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r448-reprint.pdf looks like it might be helpful, but I haven't read it closely).
> > > >
> > > > Good luck!
> > > >
> > > > P.S. I was Dorian Lamis's doctoral mentor :)
> > > >
> > > > On Wed, Aug 25, 2021 at 7:29 PM Atanas Janackovski <atanas.ja...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Thank you Pat.
> > > > >
> > > > > So, the research question is related to testing the Interpersonal Psychological Theory of Suicide (IPTS) in a non-experimental clinical sample. See picture of purported path model below. The theory states that four factors: perceived burdensomeness, thwarted belongingness, hopelessness and acquired capability are necessary and required to lead to suicide. It also states, that address thwarted belongingness or perceived burdensomeness will lead to reductions in suicidal desire. However, depression is also commonly associated with suicidality.
> > > > >
> > > > > Most the research has been cross-sectional in nature, even the ones that include more than one time point (including some I have been involved in). The models that have tested this before are mediated regression that used change scores to predicted change in suicidality. However, the underlying assumption to this type of "outcome" research, is that indeed the factors posited by the IPTS do indeed lead to suicidality. But, as most research is cross-sectional in nature, it has not looked at time-to-time changes in these factors. One recent study has used the RI-CLPM to ask this question, using beginning, mid and end point data from an RCT clinical intervention (Abbott, et. al., 2021). They found that the theory doesn't hold, that is, that changes in the theoretical variables don't predict changes in suicidality.
> > > > >
> > > > > Regarding missing data, data for some participants is MNAR, because they have completed therapy after 2, 3, … n, sessions. For others, they will continue beyond the 5 waves that I am wanting to test (but may have missing data between sessions 2–4 for other reasons, although there is not too much missing in this regard, apart from one questionnaire not being complete, for example). I have the total sessions each person attended over their episode of therapy and was entering this as covariate loading onto the random intercepts (as well as age, sex, and acquired capability as baseline [as it was only measured once in the sample, and is theoretically consistent to only measure once as it is more 'trait' like]).
> > > > >
> > > > > So, given this, is there any reason that I cannot use a RI-CLPM? If it is related to MNAR, what is the approach to this? Multiple imputation? Or is the design not able to be carried out at all?
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm not sure if it is helpful or not, but have posted my code below just in case…
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks again for your help, and please let me know if you need any more information about by questions.
> > > > >
> > > > > Interpersonal Psychological Theory of Suicide
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > (Van Orden, et. al, 2010)
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Model specification
> > > > >
> > > > > This was developed with the help of the Mulder and Hamaker (2020) article and example code.
> > > > >
> > > > > riclpm_byc_si_cov <- '
> > > > >   ## Create between components (random intercepts)
> > > > >   RIpb  =~ 1*pb_1 + 1*pb_2 + 1*pb_3 + 1*pb_4 + 1*pb_5
> > > > >   RItb  =~ 1*tb_1 + 1*tb_2 + 1*tb_3 + 1*tb_4 + 1*tb_5
> > > > >   RIbhs =~ 1*bhs_1 + 1*bhs_2 + 1*bhs_3 + 1*bhs_4 + 1*bhs_5
> > > > >   RIdep =~ 1*dep_1 + 1*dep_2 + 1*dep_3 + 1*dep_4 + 1*dep_5
> > > > >   RIsi  =~ 1*si_1 + 1*si_2 + 1*si_3 + 1*si_4 + 1*si_5
> > > > >   ## Create within-person centered variables
> > > > >   wpb_1 =~ 1*pb_1
> > > > >   wpb_2 =~ 1*pb_2
> > > > >   wpb_3 =~ 1*pb_3
> > > > >   wpb_4 =~ 1*pb_4
> > > > >   wpb_5 =~ 1*pb_5
> > > > >   ## ==
> > > > >   wtb_1 =~ 1*tb_1
> > > > >   wtb_2 =~ 1*tb_2
> > > > >   wtb_3 =~ 1*tb_3
> > > > >   wtb_4 =~ 1*tb_4
> > > > >   wtb_5 =~ 1*tb_5
> > > > >   ## ==
> > > > >   wbhs_1 =~ 1*bhs_1
> > > > >   wbhs_2 =~ 1*bhs_2
> > > > >   wbhs_3 =~ 1*bhs_3
> > > > >   wbhs_4 =~ 1*bhs_4
> > > > >   wbhs_5 =~ 1*bhs_5
> > > > >   ## ==
> > > > >   wdep_1 =~ 1*dep_1
> > > > >   wdep_2 =~ 1*dep_2
> > > > >   wdep_3 =~ 1*dep_3
> > > > >   wdep_4 =~ 1*dep_4
> > > > >   wdep_5 =~ 1*dep_5
> > > > >   ## ==
> > > > >   wsi_1 =~ 1*si_1
> > > > >   wsi_2 =~ 1*si_2
> > > > >   wsi_3 =~ 1*si_3
> > > > >   wsi_4 =~ 1*si_4
> > > > >   wsi_5 =~ 1*si_5
> > > > >   ##
> > > > >   ## =======
> > > > >   ## covariates
> > > > >   ## =======
> > > > >   ## Regression of random intercepts on covariates.
> > > > >   ## -------
> > > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ ac_1 # Constrained over time.
> > > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ age
> > > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ sex_mf
> > > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ cov_sess
> > > > >   ## =====
> > > > >   ##
> > > > >   ## Estimate the lagged effects between the within-person centered variables.
> > > > >   wpb_2 + wtb_2 + wbhs_2 + wdep_2 + wsi_2 ~ wpb_1 + wtb_1 + wbhs_1 + wdep_1 + wsi_1
> > > > >   wpb_3 + wtb_3 + wbhs_3 + wdep_3 + wsi_3 ~ wpb_2 + wtb_2 + wbhs_2 + wdep_2 + wsi_2
> > > > >   wpb_4 + wtb_4 + wbhs_4 + wdep_4 + wsi_4 ~ wpb_3 + wtb_3 + wbhs_3 + wdep_3 + wsi_3
> > > > >   wpb_5 + wtb_5 + wbhs_5 + wdep_5 + wsi_5 ~ wpb_4 + wtb_4 + wbhs_4 + wdep_4 + wsi_4
> > > > >   ## ==
> > > > >   ## Estimate the covariance between the within-person centered variables
> > > > >   ## at the first wave.
> > > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wtb_1 # Covariance
> > > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wbhs_1
> > > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wdep_1
> > > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wsi_1
> > > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wbhs_1
> > > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wdep_1
> > > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wsi_1
> > > > >   wbhs_1 ~~ wsi_1
> > > > >   wbhs_1 ~~ wdep_1
> > > > >   wdep_1 ~~ wsi_1
> > > > >   ## Estimate the covariances between the residuals of the within-person
> > > > >   ## centered variables (the innovations).
> > > > >   ## time_2
> > > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wtb_2
> > > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wbhs_2
> > > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wdep_2
> > > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wsi_2
> > > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wbhs_2
> > > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wdep_2
> > > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wsi_2
> > > > >   wbhs_2 ~~ wsi_2
> > > > >   wbhs_2 ~~ wdep_2
> > > > >   wdep_2 ~~ wsi_2
> > > > >   ## time_3
> > > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wtb_3
> > > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wbhs_3
> > > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wdep_3
> > > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wsi_3
> > > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wbhs_3
> > > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wdep_3
> > > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wsi_3
> > > > >   wbhs_3 ~~ wsi_3
> > > > >   wbhs_3 ~~ wdep_3
> > > > >   wdep_3 ~~ wsi_3
> > > > >   ## time_4
> > > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wtb_4
> > > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wbhs_4
> > > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wdep_4
> > > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wsi_4
> > > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wbhs_4
> > > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wdep_4
> > > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wsi_4
> > > > >   wbhs_4 ~~ wsi_4
> > > > >   wbhs_4 ~~ wdep_4
> > > > >   wdep_4 ~~ wsi_4
> > > > >   ## time_5
> > > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wtb_5
> > > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wbhs_5
> > > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wdep_5
> > > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wsi_5
> > > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wbhs_5
> > > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wdep_5
> > > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wsi_5
> > > > >   wbhs_5 ~~ wsi_5
> > > > >   wbhs_5 ~~ wdep_5
> > > > >   wdep_5 ~~ wsi_5
> > > > >   ## Estimate the variance and covariance of the random intercepts.
> > > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIpb
> > > > >   RItb  ~~ RItb
> > > > >   RIbhs ~~ RIbhs
> > > > >   RIdep ~~ RIdep
> > > > >   RIsi  ~~ RIsi
> > > > >   ## ==
> > > > >   RIpb  ~~ RItb
> > > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIbhs
> > > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIdep
> > > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIsi
> > > > >   RItb  ~~ RIbhs
> > > > >   RItb  ~~ RIdep
> > > > >   RItb  ~~ RIsi
> > > > >   RIbhs ~~ RIsi
> > > > >   RIbhs ~~ RIdep
> > > > >   RIdep ~~ RIsi
> > > > >   ## Estimate the (residual) variance of the within-person centered variables.
> > > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wpb_1 # Variances
> > > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wtb_1
> > > > >   wbhs_1 ~~ wbhs_1
> > > > >   wdep_1 ~~ wdep_1
> > > > >   wsi_1  ~~ wsi_1
> > > > >   ## time_2
> > > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wpb_2 # Residual variances
> > > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wtb_2
> > > > >   wbhs_2 ~~ wbhs_2
> > > > >   wdep_2 ~~ wdep_2
> > > > >   wsi_2  ~~ wsi_2
> > > > >   ## time_3
> > > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wpb_3 # Residual variances
> > > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wtb_3
> > > > >   wbhs_3 ~~ wbhs_3
> > > > >   wdep_3 ~~ wdep_3
> > > > >   wsi_3  ~~ wsi_3
> > > > >   ## time_4
> > > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wpb_4 # Residual variances
> > > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wtb_4
> > > > >   wbhs_4 ~~ wbhs_4
> > > > >   wdep_4 ~~ wdep_4
> > > > >   wsi_4  ~~ wsi_4
> > > > >   ## time_5
> > > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wpb_5 # Residual variances
> > > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wtb_5
> > > > >   wbhs_5 ~~ wbhs_5
> > > > >   wdep_5 ~~ wdep_5
> > > > >   wsi_5  ~~ wsi_5
> > > > > '
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > References
> > > > >
> > > > > Abbott, C. H., Zisk, A., Herres, J., Diamond, G. S., Krauthamer Ewing, S., & Kobak, R. (2021). Exploring the relations between interpersonal risk and adolescent suicidality during treatment. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 89(6), 528–536. doi: 10/gmkb5v
> > > > >
> > > > > Mulder, J.D. & Hamaker, E.L. (2020). Three extensions of the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model <https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10705511.2020.1784738>. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, DOI: 10.1080/10705511.2020.1784738
> > > > >
> > > > > Van Orden, K. A., Witte, T. K., Cukrowicz, K. C., Braithwaite, S. R., Selby, E. A., & Joiner, T. E. (2010). The interpersonal theory of suicide. Psychological Review, 117(2), 575–600. https://doi.org/10/b44zs2

On Thu, 26 Aug 2021 at 10:57 pm, 'Pat Malone' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> I would look at the general methods for MNAR. We're getting beyond my expertise.
>
> On Thu, Aug 26, 2021 at 7:56 AM Atanas Janackovski <atanas.ja...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Oh, thanks for the clarification. Can you recommend any resources for me to learn more about censoring processes in missingness models?
> >
> >
> > On Thu, 26 Aug 2021 at 9:48 pm, 'Pat Malone' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > > Unfortunately, that  sensitivity analysis will only distinguish between MCAR and MAR.
> > >
> > > Your missingness model may need to include a censoring process, but if you're doing a full missingness strategy for MNAR, that shouldn't be much of an extra issue.
> > >
> > > On Thu, Aug 26, 2021 at 7:34 AM Atanas Janackovski <atanas.ja...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Thank you Pat. I've been looking at some approaches using the mice package  under MNAR, but I will look into these too.
> > > >
> > > > I've started a sensitivity analysis by dropping the observations with missing data and the pattern of results so far is similar.
> > > >
> > > > I'm glad that an RI-CLPM will be usable because I think this approach suits the aims of the study. But is it still okay that I only stop at 5 waves, even for those have more sessions?
> > > >
> > > > Thanks again.
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, 26 Aug 2021 at 9:23 pm, 'Pat Malone' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > > > > Atanas,
> > > > >
> > > > > The fact that you're using RI-CLPM isn't a problem. It just means that some of the simpler solutions to your missingness problem won't be helpful. I don't  have specific suggestions for techniques to model the non-random missing with your SEM, but you might try the work of Craig Enders or Karthika Mohan (e.g., https://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r448-reprint.pdf looks like it might be helpful, but I haven't read it closely).
> > > > >
> > > > > Good luck!
> > > > >
> > > > > P.S. I was Dorian Lamis's doctoral mentor :)
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wed, Aug 25, 2021 at 7:29 PM Atanas Janackovski <atanas.ja...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Thank you Pat.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > So, the research question is related to testing the Interpersonal Psychological Theory of Suicide (IPTS) in a non-experimental clinical sample. See picture of purported path model below. The theory states that four factors: perceived burdensomeness, thwarted belongingness, hopelessness and acquired capability are necessary and required to lead to suicide. It also states, that address thwarted belongingness or perceived burdensomeness will lead to reductions in suicidal desire. However, depression is also commonly associated with suicidality.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Most the research has been cross-sectional in nature, even the ones that include more than one time point (including some I have been involved in). The models that have tested this before are mediated regression that used change scores to predicted change in suicidality. However, the underlying assumption to this type of "outcome" research, is that indeed the factors posited by the IPTS do indeed lead to suicidality. But, as most research is cross-sectional in nature, it has not looked at time-to-time changes in these factors. One recent study has used the RI-CLPM to ask this question, using beginning, mid and end point data from an RCT clinical intervention (Abbott, et. al., 2021). They found that the theory doesn't hold, that is, that changes in the theoretical variables don't predict changes in suicidality.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Regarding missing data, data for some participants is MNAR, because they have completed therapy after 2, 3, … n, sessions. For others, they will continue beyond the 5 waves that I am wanting to test (but may have missing data between sessions 2–4 for other reasons, although there is not too much missing in this regard, apart from one questionnaire not being complete, for example). I have the total sessions each person attended over their episode of therapy and was entering this as covariate loading onto the random intercepts (as well as age, sex, and acquired capability as baseline [as it was only measured once in the sample, and is theoretically consistent to only measure once as it is more 'trait' like]).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > So, given this, is there any reason that I cannot use a RI-CLPM? If it is related to MNAR, what is the approach to this? Multiple imputation? Or is the design not able to be carried out at all?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I'm not sure if it is helpful or not, but have posted my code below just in case…
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks again for your help, and please let me know if you need any more information about by questions.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Interpersonal Psychological Theory of Suicide
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > (Van Orden, et. al, 2010)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Model specification
> > > > > >
> > > > > > This was developed with the help of the Mulder and Hamaker (2020) article and example code.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > riclpm_byc_si_cov <- '
> > > > > >   ## Create between components (random intercepts)
> > > > > >   RIpb  =~ 1*pb_1 + 1*pb_2 + 1*pb_3 + 1*pb_4 + 1*pb_5
> > > > > >   RItb  =~ 1*tb_1 + 1*tb_2 + 1*tb_3 + 1*tb_4 + 1*tb_5
> > > > > >   RIbhs =~ 1*bhs_1 + 1*bhs_2 + 1*bhs_3 + 1*bhs_4 + 1*bhs_5
> > > > > >   RIdep =~ 1*dep_1 + 1*dep_2 + 1*dep_3 + 1*dep_4 + 1*dep_5
> > > > > >   RIsi  =~ 1*si_1 + 1*si_2 + 1*si_3 + 1*si_4 + 1*si_5
> > > > > >   ## Create within-person centered variables
> > > > > >   wpb_1 =~ 1*pb_1
> > > > > >   wpb_2 =~ 1*pb_2
> > > > > >   wpb_3 =~ 1*pb_3
> > > > > >   wpb_4 =~ 1*pb_4
> > > > > >   wpb_5 =~ 1*pb_5
> > > > > >   ## ==
> > > > > >   wtb_1 =~ 1*tb_1
> > > > > >   wtb_2 =~ 1*tb_2
> > > > > >   wtb_3 =~ 1*tb_3
> > > > > >   wtb_4 =~ 1*tb_4
> > > > > >   wtb_5 =~ 1*tb_5
> > > > > >   ## ==
> > > > > >   wbhs_1 =~ 1*bhs_1
> > > > > >   wbhs_2 =~ 1*bhs_2
> > > > > >   wbhs_3 =~ 1*bhs_3
> > > > > >   wbhs_4 =~ 1*bhs_4
> > > > > >   wbhs_5 =~ 1*bhs_5
> > > > > >   ## ==
> > > > > >   wdep_1 =~ 1*dep_1
> > > > > >   wdep_2 =~ 1*dep_2
> > > > > >   wdep_3 =~ 1*dep_3
> > > > > >   wdep_4 =~ 1*dep_4
> > > > > >   wdep_5 =~ 1*dep_5
> > > > > >   ## ==
> > > > > >   wsi_1 =~ 1*si_1
> > > > > >   wsi_2 =~ 1*si_2
> > > > > >   wsi_3 =~ 1*si_3
> > > > > >   wsi_4 =~ 1*si_4
> > > > > >   wsi_5 =~ 1*si_5
> > > > > >   ##
> > > > > >   ## =======
> > > > > >   ## covariates
> > > > > >   ## =======
> > > > > >   ## Regression of random intercepts on covariates.
> > > > > >   ## -------
> > > > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ ac_1 # Constrained over time.
> > > > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ age
> > > > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ sex_mf
> > > > > >   RIpb + RItb + RIbhs + RIdep+ RIsi ~ cov_sess
> > > > > >   ## =====
> > > > > >   ##
> > > > > >   ## Estimate the lagged effects between the within-person centered variables.
> > > > > >   wpb_2 + wtb_2 + wbhs_2 + wdep_2 + wsi_2 ~ wpb_1 + wtb_1 + wbhs_1 + wdep_1 + wsi_1
> > > > > >   wpb_3 + wtb_3 + wbhs_3 + wdep_3 + wsi_3 ~ wpb_2 + wtb_2 + wbhs_2 + wdep_2 + wsi_2
> > > > > >   wpb_4 + wtb_4 + wbhs_4 + wdep_4 + wsi_4 ~ wpb_3 + wtb_3 + wbhs_3 + wdep_3 + wsi_3
> > > > > >   wpb_5 + wtb_5 + wbhs_5 + wdep_5 + wsi_5 ~ wpb_4 + wtb_4 + wbhs_4 + wdep_4 + wsi_4
> > > > > >   ## ==
> > > > > >   ## Estimate the covariance between the within-person centered variables
> > > > > >   ## at the first wave.
> > > > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wtb_1 # Covariance
> > > > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wbhs_1
> > > > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wdep_1
> > > > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wsi_1
> > > > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wbhs_1
> > > > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wdep_1
> > > > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wsi_1
> > > > > >   wbhs_1 ~~ wsi_1
> > > > > >   wbhs_1 ~~ wdep_1
> > > > > >   wdep_1 ~~ wsi_1
> > > > > >   ## Estimate the covariances between the residuals of the within-person
> > > > > >   ## centered variables (the innovations).
> > > > > >   ## time_2
> > > > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wtb_2
> > > > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wbhs_2
> > > > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wdep_2
> > > > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wsi_2
> > > > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wbhs_2
> > > > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wdep_2
> > > > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wsi_2
> > > > > >   wbhs_2 ~~ wsi_2
> > > > > >   wbhs_2 ~~ wdep_2
> > > > > >   wdep_2 ~~ wsi_2
> > > > > >   ## time_3
> > > > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wtb_3
> > > > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wbhs_3
> > > > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wdep_3
> > > > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wsi_3
> > > > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wbhs_3
> > > > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wdep_3
> > > > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wsi_3
> > > > > >   wbhs_3 ~~ wsi_3
> > > > > >   wbhs_3 ~~ wdep_3
> > > > > >   wdep_3 ~~ wsi_3
> > > > > >   ## time_4
> > > > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wtb_4
> > > > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wbhs_4
> > > > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wdep_4
> > > > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wsi_4
> > > > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wbhs_4
> > > > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wdep_4
> > > > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wsi_4
> > > > > >   wbhs_4 ~~ wsi_4
> > > > > >   wbhs_4 ~~ wdep_4
> > > > > >   wdep_4 ~~ wsi_4
> > > > > >   ## time_5
> > > > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wtb_5
> > > > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wbhs_5
> > > > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wdep_5
> > > > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wsi_5
> > > > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wbhs_5
> > > > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wdep_5
> > > > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wsi_5
> > > > > >   wbhs_5 ~~ wsi_5
> > > > > >   wbhs_5 ~~ wdep_5
> > > > > >   wdep_5 ~~ wsi_5
> > > > > >   ## Estimate the variance and covariance of the random intercepts.
> > > > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIpb
> > > > > >   RItb  ~~ RItb
> > > > > >   RIbhs ~~ RIbhs
> > > > > >   RIdep ~~ RIdep
> > > > > >   RIsi  ~~ RIsi
> > > > > >   ## ==
> > > > > >   RIpb  ~~ RItb
> > > > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIbhs
> > > > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIdep
> > > > > >   RIpb  ~~ RIsi
> > > > > >   RItb  ~~ RIbhs
> > > > > >   RItb  ~~ RIdep
> > > > > >   RItb  ~~ RIsi
> > > > > >   RIbhs ~~ RIsi
> > > > > >   RIbhs ~~ RIdep
> > > > > >   RIdep ~~ RIsi
> > > > > >   ## Estimate the (residual) variance of the within-person centered variables.
> > > > > >   wpb_1  ~~ wpb_1 # Variances
> > > > > >   wtb_1  ~~ wtb_1
> > > > > >   wbhs_1 ~~ wbhs_1
> > > > > >   wdep_1 ~~ wdep_1
> > > > > >   wsi_1  ~~ wsi_1
> > > > > >   ## time_2
> > > > > >   wpb_2  ~~ wpb_2 # Residual variances
> > > > > >   wtb_2  ~~ wtb_2
> > > > > >   wbhs_2 ~~ wbhs_2
> > > > > >   wdep_2 ~~ wdep_2
> > > > > >   wsi_2  ~~ wsi_2
> > > > > >   ## time_3
> > > > > >   wpb_3  ~~ wpb_3 # Residual variances
> > > > > >   wtb_3  ~~ wtb_3
> > > > > >   wbhs_3 ~~ wbhs_3
> > > > > >   wdep_3 ~~ wdep_3
> > > > > >   wsi_3  ~~ wsi_3
> > > > > >   ## time_4
> > > > > >   wpb_4  ~~ wpb_4 # Residual variances
> > > > > >   wtb_4  ~~ wtb_4
> > > > > >   wbhs_4 ~~ wbhs_4
> > > > > >   wdep_4 ~~ wdep_4
> > > > > >   wsi_4  ~~ wsi_4
> > > > > >   ## time_5
> > > > > >   wpb_5  ~~ wpb_5 # Residual variances
> > > > > >   wtb_5  ~~ wtb_5
> > > > > >   wbhs_5 ~~ wbhs_5
> > > > > >   wdep_5 ~~ wdep_5
> > > > > >   wsi_5  ~~ wsi_5
> > > > > > '

> > > > > >
> > > > > > Mulder, J.D. & Hamaker, E.L. (2020). Three extensions of the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model <https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10705511.2020.1784738>. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, DOI: 10.1080/10705511.2020.1784738
> > > > > >

> > > > > > On Thursday, August 26, 2021 at 1:08:40 AM UTC+10 Pat Malone wrote:
> > > > > > > Ah, I just saw in the SEMNET version of this question that you are interested in longitudinal analysis. In that case, I suggest more careful attention to the MAR assumption beyond just number of sessions.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Pat
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Wed, Aug 25, 2021 at 10:55 AM Pat Malone <p...@farharbor.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > Atanas,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > It would help to know more about your model (and research question).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If the participants have been discharged, there is almost certainly a reason that is not captured in the number of sessions. So if sessions are not interchangeable, data are missing not at random, meaning FIML cannot fully compensate, unless you have a lot more information in the model (perhaps from the final session?) that would contribute to knowing why the data are missing.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If sessions are interchangeable, you're probably ok with a multilevel model with sessions nested within participants, but that rules out longitudinal analyses.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Pat
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Wed, Aug 25, 2021 at 9:40 AM Atanas Janackovski <atanas.ja...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Hi, this is more a stats question than a lavaan question, but given I am using lavaan, thought I may as well ask it here… Apologies if this is not okay. Here goes…
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I have data from people attending psychological therapy in a non-experimental setting. As this is a naturalistic setting, participants attend a different number of sessions. The sample size is N = 639, with mean number of session of 5.24 (SD = 2.16, range = 2–13).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I want to test a number of different variables, and have included the total number of sessions attended as a covariate in the analysis (for the random intercept at least). I am using the R package lavaan, using "full information maximum likelihood" to estimate the missing data. So, for someone that has been discharged after 2 sessions, lavaan will handle the "missing" data.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > My question is, can I actually use this type of analysis with this data set? Are there any assumptions I am violating by specifying the model this way?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I have searched the internet as well as looked for primary sources, however I cannot seem to find anything to help me. Please let me know if you need more information about my questions.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Thanks in advance.

messages.subject: Re: Interpreting and dealing with nonsignificant results of CFA
messages.subject_clean: Interpreting and dealing with nonsignificant results of CFA
messages.body_plain:
> Do you suggest any way to find a better model fit?

You have to be willing to consider that the theory is wrong or insufficiently complex, at least in the context in which these data were gathered.  As Xavier noted, the items might function differently across cultures, but there have also been instances of mistranslation or inequality of meaning across languages.

Empirically, you can see which specific pairwise relationships the model fails to reproduce closely.  Use lavResiduals() to inspect the matrix of standardized residuals, and read the reference(s) listed there to understand how to interpret them.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: How to get the factor correlation matrix in case of imputed data
messages.subject_clean: How to get the factor correlation matrix in case of imputed data
messages.body_plain:
> I actually have no idea if there is any convenient way to extract the factor correlation matrix. It seems that 'lavinspect(fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv/>")' does not work in the case of imputed data sets.

Correct, there is no analogous option for a class?lavaan.mi object.  You just have to look at the standardized solution in the summary() method.

Caveat:  If you use std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, then the estimated factor covariances are already correlations, so you could save the lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv/>") ouput for each imputation and average the matrices using Reduce().  Extending the help-page example:

HSMiss <- HolzingerSwineford1939[ , c(paste("x", 1:9, sep = ""),
                                      "ageyr","agemo","school")]
set.seed(12345)
HSMiss$x5 <- ifelse(HSMiss$x5 <= quantile(HSMiss$x5, .3), NA, HSMiss$x5)
age <- HSMiss$ageyr + HSMiss$agemo/12
HSMiss$x9 <- ifelse(age <= quantile(age, .3), NA, HSMiss$x9)

## specify CFA model from lavaan's ?cfa help page
HS.model <- '
  visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
  speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
'
## function to save list of extra output per imputation
getCors <- function(x) {
  list(LV = lavInspect(x, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>"), ALL = lavInspect(x, "cor.all"))
}
## impute data within runMI
nImps <- 20
out <- cfa.mi(HS.model, data = HSMiss, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
              FUN = getCors, m = nImps, seed = 12345,
              miArgs = list(noms = "school"))
## pool latent correlation matrices
Reduce("+", lapply(out@funList, function(x) x$LV))  / nImps
## pool latent+observed correlation matrices
Reduce("+", lapply(out@funList, function(x) x$ALL))  / nImps

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Great!

> does the use of these orthonormal contrast codes change the interpretation of the findings in any significant way that I should keep in mind?

Yes, the tests of linear, quadratic, etc. effects are valid, but you lose the simple interpretation of "a 1-unit increase in time is associated with an expected change of [slope] units in the outcome."  Essentially, the best way to interpret the results will be visually.  Pick your preferred model that balances complexity and parsimony, then calculate the expected marginal means for each timepoint (i.e., multiply the growth-factor means by the loading for each occasion).  If you store them in a vector, you can plot them against time.

> I fit a model that included some latent interactions using data with just over 600 observations with some missing data.

Multiple latent interactions, using product indicators?  Sounds like a complex model for only 600 observations.  How many variables, including product indicators?

> The model itself on the original data worked well

What does that mean?  A model without interactions / product indicators?

> but then I simulated sample data using the simulateData() command and parameters from the original data. > Not that I am aware of; you just pick up R tricks over the years.  The function is typically used to calculate an outer product of two vectors (i.e., the resulting matrix is the product of all combinations among the 2 vectors).  The FUN= argument simply allows a different operation to be performed on all combinations between 2 vectors.  More general combinations can be manipulated similarly using the combn() function (e.g., for every combination of 3 values out of a set of 5 values, do some function).

Then write a 2-argument function to do what you want for each ColA--RowB combination (and a third argument to name the user-defined parameter created by each combination?). This part:

"Moreover, when Predictor 1 and Predictor2 are tested Together as predictors - there is no indirect effect observed for either."

Is not at all surprising if 1 and 2 are correlated.It's the same shared variance issue as in any multiple regression framework.

This part:

"But when Predictor 1 is multiplied by Predictor 2, to create a new Predictor variable, we will call Predictor X. This is NOT observed to have an indirect effect. This runs against my expectation."

The most likely scenarios here are that the test is under-powered or your hypothesis about X is incorrect. Are 1 and 2 included in the model with X? If not, they should be. Again, same as in any multiple regression.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: Mediation muddle
messages.subject_clean: Mediation muddle
messages.body_plain:
In a regression framework, if you include a higher-order term (e.g., a two-way interaction), you need to also include the lower-order/component terms in the same model as predictors of the same things.

So don't just run

Y ~ PX

Run

Y ~ PX + P1 + P2

If this still doesn't make sense, I suggest hitting up a text like Cohen, Cohen, Aiken, & West's book on multiple regression. It's very clear on how to work with interactions and most of the principles generalize directly to a path/structural framework.

Pat

messages.body_plain:
Hey yall, I am at my wits end and do not understand why the summary function in lavaan (v0.6-7) isn't giving me all the information it used to (i.e., back in May when I ran the same code). I found support for noninvariance up to scalar but when I try to get the intercepts to determine if there are significant differences in latent scores for my group, the summary does not give me any signifance values. This is the code I used:

DASS [,c("DA1","DA2","DA3","DA4","DA5","DA6","DA7","DA8","DA9","DA10","DA11","DA12","DA13","DA14","DA15","DA16","DA17","DA18","DA19","DA20","DA21")] <- lapply(DASS [,c("DA1","DA2","DA3","DA4","DA5","DA6","DA7","DA8","DA9","DA10","DA11","DA12","DA13","DA14","DA15","DA16","DA17","DA18","DA19","DA20","DA21")],ordered)

DASS_imp<-mice(DASS, m = 20, method = "pmm")
mice.imp<- NULL
for(i in 1:20) { mice.imp[[i]] <- complete(DASS_imp, action=i, inc=FALSE)
}

fitscalar <- cfa.mi(CFA,estimator="wlsmv", data=mice.imp,group="trans", group.equal=c("loadings","intercepts"))
fitMeasures(fitscalar, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "rmsea"))
summary(fitscalar)

I did not have this problem before the and the summary function used to give me the full output but now it is only giving me "est.ave":
Group 2 []:

Latent Variables:
                    est.ave
  stress =~
    DA1               1.000
    DA6     (.p2.)    1.120
    DA8     (.p3.)    1.191
    DA11    (.p4.)    1.254
    DA12    (.p5.)    1.266

    DA18    (.p7.)    1.102
  anx =~
    DA2               1.000

    DA15    (.12.)    2.161

    DA20    (.14.)    2.038

    DA3               1.000

    DA10    (.17.)    1.018
    DA13    (.18.)    0.955
    DA16    (.19.)    1.009
    DA17    (.20.)    1.003
    DA21    (.21.)    1.011

Covariances:
                    est.ave
  stress ~~
    anx               0.208
    dep               0.400
  anx ~~
    dep               0.254

Intercepts:
                    est.ave
   .DA1               0.000
   .DA6               0.000
   .DA8               0.000
   .DA11              0.000
   .DA12              0.000
   .DA14              0.000

   .DA21              0.000
    stress            0.161
    anx               0.156
    dep               0.359

Please let me know what I am doing wrong.

THANK YOU!,
Louis Lindley (a very lost PhD student)

messages.body_plain:
Pat - I have access to pretty much all journals, but no books.
Not to worry if you can't - but if you can, could you recommend any journal article (e.g. a review) for this aspect: (or keywords/key terms to try and track down such an article):  or a website even:
----------------------

"In a regression framework, if you include a higher-order term (e.g., a two-way interaction), you need to also include the lower-order/component
terms in the same model as predictors of the same things.
So don't just run
Y ~ PX
Run
Y ~ PX + P1 + P2"

---------------------
Thanks Pat - and again, not to worry if you can't.
And don't go to any trouble - just if such a reference is at the top of your mind.

On Friday, August 27, 2021 at 3:13:37 PM UTC-3 Pat Malone wrote:
> You do need to do some homework, but yes, the indirect effect of PX should be interpretable in the model you describe.
>
> On Fri, Aug 27, 2021 at 1:50 PM Mikelavaan <mikeyf...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > And further to my last message (which you might not have seen yet):
> > when I look at the results, I am just looking at the indirect effect for Predictor X (whether 0 is in the CI or not)?
> > Because in the results (when I do as in my last message, which you might not have seen yet), I DO see an indirect effect for Predictor X (0 is not in the CI).
> > But NOT for Predictor 1 or Predictor 2 (for each, 0 is observed within the CI).
> >
> > Predictor X is the point of interest here.
> > Because for Predictors 1 and 2 - I can analyze them seperately (and each seperately do show an indirect effect).
> >
> > On Friday, August 27, 2021 at 2:31:58 PM UTC-3 Mikelavaan wrote:
> > > I will have to do some reading to understand why.
> > > But I think I understand what you mean: so this is what I have to do the mediation analysis with:
> > >
> > > PREDICTORS
> > > Predictor X
> > > Predictor 1
> > > Predictor 2
> > >
> > > MEDIATOR
> > > Mediation variable
> > >
> > > DEPENDENT
> > > Dependent variable
> > >
> > > Is that correct?
> > > I cannot just use Predictor X alone as a sole predictor.
> > > The things that went into forming Predictor X need to be put as predictors in addition: Predictor 1 and Predictor 2.
> > >
> > > On Friday, August 27, 2021 at 1:58:45 PM UTC-3 Pat Malone wrote:
> > > > In a regression framework, if you include a higher-order term (e.g., a two-way interaction), you need to also include the lower-order/component terms in the same model as predictors of the same things.
> > > >
> > > > So don't just run
> > > >
> > > > Y ~ PX
> > > >
> > > > Run
> > > >
> > > > Y ~ PX + P1 + P2
> > > >
> > > > If this still doesn't make sense, I suggest hitting up a text like Cohen, Cohen, Aiken, & West's book on multiple regression. It's very clear on how to work with interactions and most of the principles generalize directly to a path/structural framework.
> > > >
> > > > Pat
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Fri, Aug 27, 2021 at 12:10 PM Mikelavaan <mikeyf...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Pat - thank you. that is super helpful.
> > > > > But one part I didn't understand, where you write: "Are 1 and 2 included in the model with X? "
> > > > > Predictor X is just (Predictor 1*Predictor 2). i.e. each value of Predictor 1 multipled by the corresponding value of Predictor 2.
> > > > >
> > > > > But Predictor X (unlike Predictor 1, and unlike Predictor 2) does not have an indirect effect. (with the same Mediator and Dependent variables).
> > > > >
> > > > > On Friday, August 27, 2021 at 12:39:57 PM UTC-3 Pat Malone wrote:
> > > > > > This part:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > "Moreover, when Predictor 1 and Predictor2 are tested Together as predictors - there is no indirect effect observed for either."
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Is not at all surprising if 1 and 2 are correlated.It's the same shared variance issue as in any multiple regression framework.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > This part:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > "But when Predictor 1 is multiplied by Predictor 2, to create a new Predictor variable, we will call Predictor X. This is NOT observed to have an indirect effect. This runs against my expectation."
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The most likely scenarios here are that the test is under-powered or your hypothesis about X is incorrect. Are 1 and 2 included in the model with X? If not, they should be. Again, same as in any multiple regression.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Pat
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Fri, Aug 27, 2021 at 8:55 AM Mikelavaan <mikeyf...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Does the following scenario surprise anyone? It is my situation, which I am a bit perplexed by.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Using JASP, which runs lavaan:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I have a situation where Predictor 1 is shown to have an indirect effect, via Mediator, on dependent variable.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > And when tested seperately, Predictor 2 is shown to have an indirect effect, via the same Mediator, on the same dependent variable.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > But when Predictor 1 is multiplied by Predictor 2, to create a new Predictor variable, we will call Predictor X. This is NOT observed to have an indirect effect. This runs against my expectation.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Moreover, when Predictor 1 and Predictor2 are tested Together as predictors - there is no indirect effect observed for either.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Is it just that my expectations are ill placed?

Yep, that is what I meant by syntax. Thank you.

I see with the DASS that you pass to mice, you are considering the items to be ordered. Are you telling Lavaan that they are ordered? And, if you are treating them as ordered, then I think you would want to constrain the item thresholds and not the intercepts.

You could try using the measEQ.syntax function in the semTools package to write out the specific models you want to test, or you could try adding the constraints manually to your lavaan syntax and see if that resolves your issue.

You might find something in an "Annual Review of ..." journal (Psychology, Sociology, see https://www.annualreviews.org/ ), whch often have methods chapters. Or an online course, many of which are free. That's about as far as I can take it. Good lucck!

> Pat - I have access to pretty much all journals, but no books.
> Not to worry if you can't - but if you can, could you recommend any journal article (e.g. a review) for this aspect: (or keywords/key terms to try and track down such an article):  or a website even:
> ----------------------
> "In a regression framework, if you include a higher-order term (e.g., a two-way interaction), you need to also include the lower-order/component
> terms in the same model as predictors of the same things.
> So don't just run
> Y ~ PX
> Run
> Y ~ PX + P1 + P2"
> ---------------------
> Thanks Pat - and again, not to worry if you can't.
> And don't go to any trouble - just if such a reference is at the top of your mind.

> > You do need to do some homework, but yes, the indirect effect of PX should be interpretable in the model you describe.
> >
> > On Fri, Aug 27, 2021 at 1:50 PM Mikelavaan <mikeyf...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > And further to my last message (which you might not have seen yet):
> > > when I look at the results, I am just looking at the indirect effect for Predictor X (whether 0 is in the CI or not)?
> > > Because in the results (when I do as in my last message, which you might not have seen yet), I DO see an indirect effect for Predictor X (0 is not in the CI).
> > > But NOT for Predictor 1 or Predictor 2 (for each, 0 is observed within the CI).
> > >
> > > Predictor X is the point of interest here.
> > > Because for Predictors 1 and 2 - I can analyze them seperately (and each seperately do show an indirect effect).

> > > >
> > > > PREDICTORS
> > > > Predictor X
> > > > Predictor 1
> > > > Predictor 2
> > > >
> > > > MEDIATOR
> > > > Mediation variable
> > > >
> > > > DEPENDENT
> > > > Dependent variable
> > > >
> > > > Is that correct?
> > > > I cannot just use Predictor X alone as a sole predictor.
> > > > The things that went into forming Predictor X need to be put as predictors in addition: Predictor 1 and Predictor 2.
> > > >
> > > > On Friday, August 27, 2021 at 1:58:45 PM UTC-3 Pat Malone wrote:
> > > > > In a regression framework, if you include a higher-order term (e.g., a two-way interaction), you need to also include the lower-order/component terms in the same model as predictors of the same things.
> > > > >
> > > > > So don't just run
> > > > >
> > > > > Y ~ PX
> > > > >
> > > > > Run
> > > > >

> > > > > Pat
> > > > >
> > > > >

messages.subject: Re: Using bounds and optim.bound to constrain the range of parameter estimation
messages.subject_clean: Using bounds and optim.bound to constrain the range of parameter estimation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence,

Thanks for your feedback.

Yes, lavaan's model syntax is powerful and straightforward in the use of labeled parameters to impose equality and inequality constraints.

Please allow me to clarify the matter:

In the investigation of the possible cause(s) of negative residual variance in one variable, I have tried solutions equivalent to your example but lavaan has nevertheless returned negative residual variance even when it is is constrained > 0 if bounds="none" (lavaan default); the same negative residual variance happened even if constrained == 0.

If bounds="standard", the residual variance is nonnegative but factor variance is constrained to equality between groups (even though factor variance is explicitly allowed to differ between groups in the model syntax). That's the reason of the query on `bounds` and `optim.bounds`.

Issues with constrained parameter estimation are well known (e.g.  Savalei & Kolenikov 2008; Kolenikov & Bollen 2012). The aim is just to investigate what might be happening with this group in this specific survey, using a range of options, for referees may inquiry about this negative variance parameter for this one group-year -- which is not unexpected given the SEMNET skirmishes on the causes of negative residual variance.

Best,
Fabricio

messages.subject: Re: Guidelines for invariance with skewed continuous predictors
messages.subject_clean: Guidelines for invariance with skewed continuous predictors
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Conal.

Sorry this took a bit.

I'm not going to address fit indices, except to say the pros and cons are pretty much the same, though some that you're used to might not be available in DWLS.

As long as your invariance strategy is appropriate to ordered indicators, you're fine. Terrence Jorgensen has many posts on the subject in the archives, including recently, posting this reference

Kite, B. A., Jorgensen, T. D., & Chen, P. Y. (2018). Random permutation testing applied to measurement invariance testing with ordered-categorical indicators. *Structural Equation Modeling, 25*(4), 573--587. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2017.1421467

If the hurdle variable is the outcome, it's really not that bad. Try looking on the keyword "semicontinuous outcomes." There's quite a lot out there.

blavaan (note case) handles odd distributions just fine. But only model comparisons are available--you won't get fit indices. Instead you'll look at WAIC, LOO, Bayes factors, etc. But for invariance testing, that's what you need.

Pat

On Tue, Aug 24, 2021 at 8:54 PM Conal Monaghan <conal.m...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks for the reply. Definately WLS is difficult but maybe the best approach is DWLS going forward and try to remove as much of the skewed items as possible. Would there be any downside to DWLS over MLR in terms of interpreting fit indicies using the same criteria or implimenting invariance analyses?
>
> I agree that anything with a hurdle is much more difficult. When this is the case, we could consider splitting data seperately for both groups (smokers / non-smokers) within your example.
>
> Blavaan could be a good option, would this be approapriate for most non-normal underlying distributions / count variables? Similarly to DWLS, are you aware of interpreting BLavaan models in line with standard fit criteria (CFI,NNFI, RMSEA, SRMR) or Invariance modelling (through comparing CFI change).
>
> Cheers,
> Conal
>
> On Sunday, August 1, 2021 at 11:06:35 PM UTC+10 Pat Malone wrote:
> > Conal,
> >
> > ML assumes data are multivariate normal. MLR allows for heavy tails, but does not help with the kind of floor effect and skew you are facing.
> >
> > WLS is usually considered unstable at best without sample sizes of at least 5,000.
> >
> > I think your best bet if you want to stay in lavaan is binning your indicators (e.g., 0 to capture the floor, then quartiles among what remains) and using DWLS.
> >
> > Another possibility is blavaan to avoid the distributional assumptions.
> >
> > Though if your data have a hurdle process you might want to try to model that, but that's trickier. Example: If the variable is number of cigarettes smoked, zero is qualitatively different from 1 and up--the data-generating process has to cross a "hurdle" to get from the binary (0 / >0) part to the continuous part.
> >
> > Pat
> >
> > On Sat, Jul 31, 2021 at 11:56 PM Conal Monaghan <conal.m...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi Everyone,
> > > We have been looking for clear guidelines for investigating invariance with heavily skewed continuous predictors.
> > >
> > > Although we are curious about general principles, the case we are looking at is a three factor structure with three different targets of the questions (rules for self, men, woman). We are treating this as longitudinal model, as each participant completes all three scales (equivalence of the same structure across all three targets / within subjects; i.e., using longFacNames and long.equal within measEq.syntax() ). (No Minimal reproducible example given theoretical discussion and guidelines).
> > >
> > > Example indicator distribution attached.
> > >
> > > 1. When modelling a standard CFA for each model individually, it appears that WLS are better indicated given the distribution of some of the indicators. ML/MLR are strong methods of obtaining parameters when distributions are closer to normal, however, when this is substantially violated, WLS is better - essentially treating the indicators as ordinal. Given difficulties with converging, DWLS is often used here. (Forero et al., 2009; https://doi.org/10.1080/10705510903203573).
> > >
> > > When taking this approach, would we need to specify all indicators as categorical (Note that here we are using 0-100, however, often Likert 1-7 is used), and do the standard alternative fit indices make sense (SRMR, RMSEA, CFI, NNFI)?
> > >
> > > 2. However, when then running invariance through standard sequential constraint of parameters, it is unclear whether the standard approach to change in CFI is still meaningful using DWLS and not ML/MLR. Can we still use change in CFI at .01 (liberal) and .005 / .002 being more stringent benchmarks for change.
> > >
> > >
> > > With Kind Regards and thanks for your help in advance,
> > >     Conal Monaghan

messages.subject: Re: Using bounds and optim.bound to constrain the range of parameter estimation
messages.subject_clean: Using bounds and optim.bound to constrain the range of parameter estimation
messages.body_plain:
One big caveat here is that if you use (linear) equality constraints,
the bounds do not work any more.

(The reason is that in the presence of linear equality constraints, the
constrained parameter vector is projected to a smaller but unconstrained
parameter vector; this is very efficient, but the bounds no longer have
any meaning in this projected space)

Yves.

> factor loading is slightly above one, ~1.1). The number of observations
> for the group is large enough (700+) to presume the residual variance is

> /not/ due to sampling fluctuation.

> In order to investigate the issue, among other things, I've played with

messages.subject_clean: Interpreting and dealing with nonsignificant results of CFA
messages.body_plain:
> > Do you suggest any way to find a better model fit?
>
> You have to be willing to consider that the theory is wrong or insufficiently complex, at least in the context in which these data were gathered.  As Xavier noted, the items might function differently across cultures, but there have also been instances of mistranslation or inequality of meaning across languages.
>
> Empirically, you can see which specific pairwise relationships the model fails to reproduce closely.  Use lavResiduals() to inspect the matrix of standardized residuals, and read the reference(s) listed there to understand how to interpret them.

 Thanks Terrence,
Should the covariances be less than 0.1 to be accepted as satisfactory results?

Bests,
Sara

messages.subject: Explained variance for CFA(?)
messages.subject_clean: Explained variance for CFA(?)
messages.body_plain:
Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) using fa() function provides in its output a row called Proportion Var. You can typically get the variance explained for the whole model by summing the  Proportion Var for each component. For example:

# Make EFA model
library(psych)
fit <- fa(mydata, nfactors = 4, rotate = "oblimin", scores = "Bartlett", fm = "minres")

# Get variance explained for each component
fit$Vaccounted[2,]

# Get sum of variance explained
sum(unlist(fit$Vaccounted[2,]))

My coauthor and I would like to compare this number for EFA with its equivalent for Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), but the cfa() function does not seem to provide Proportion Var per default.

So first, is there a statistical reason why the cfa() output does not provide Proportion Var or an equivalent? Should we be avoiding attempting this comparison or even obtaining explained variance for CFA at all?

Second, I have attempted to calculate this value myself through a custom function (using source 1 <https://stackoverflow.com/questions/22024700/how-can-i-extract-factor-loadings-from-lavaan/30959079> and source 2 <https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58159778/how-to-extract-percent-variance-information-from-r-class-loadings>):

mycfa <- function(data, indices) {
  d <- data[indices,]
  fit <- cfa(model, data = d, estimator = "MLR")
  inspect(fit, what = "std")$lambda -> loadings
  sum(loadings[,1]^2) -> SS.loadings
  Proportion.Var.MR1 <- sum(loadings[,1]^2)/nrow(loadings)
  Proportion.Var.MR2 <- sum(loadings[,2]^2)/nrow(loadings)
  Proportion.Var.MR3 <- sum(loadings[,3]^2)/nrow(loadings)
  Proportion.Var.MR4 <- sum(loadings[,4]^2)/nrow(loadings)
  output <- Proportion.Var.MR1 + Proportion.Var.MR2 + Proportion.Var.MR3 + Proportion.Var.MR4
  output
}

The idea would be to compare two distributions/histograms of 10,000 bootstrapped samples of the explained variances for the EFA and CFA, respectively, to see if they overlap, and to what extent. Would that approach make sense?

So to bootstrap the 10,000 explained variances for CFA, I simply use the custom function above along with the boot package:

library(boot)
(vars.boot <- boot(data = mydata, statistic = mycfa, R = 10000))

The output, however, provides 275 impossible values (out of 10,000)—i.e., values greater than 1 (the variance explained shouldn't be greater than 1). Would there be any explanation for this? That's not much, but it does seem like a problem. Is the function at fault here, or is the bootstrapping, or the combination of the two?

While running my model, I do get this warning:
In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative

But I am not sure what to do with this or what the implications are. Could this be related to the impossible bootstrapped values? Thank you very much.

Related/relevant conversations:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/tPEPXQqQR48/m/l_JfDsw5GAAJ
https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/W5rIa2eo3uQ

messages.body_plain:
> now it is only giving me "est.ave":

That is the default method for the lavaanList class, from which lavaan.mi inherits.  This suggests there is a problem with R searching the correct path to find the lavaan.mi methods.  Save your mice.imp object, e.g.,

saveRDS(mice.imp, file = "impList.rds")

Then open a fresh R session and load it, and load ONLY semTools (which already loads lavaan as a dependency, along with lavaan's dependencies).

mice.imp <- saveRDS("impList.rds")
library(semTools)

fitscalar <- cfa.mi(CFA,estimator="wlsmv", data=mice.imp,group="trans", group.equal=c("loadings","intercepts"))
fitMeasures(fitscalar, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "rmsea"))
summary(fitscalar)

Does it work then?  If so, I would like to know what other packages were showing up in your sessionInfo(), which might have interfered with semTools.

I think the generalization to CFA (or oblique factors more generally) is the average variance explained (AVE), which is available from most lavaan objects with latent variables (EFA or CFA) from semTools::reliability()

You could also look at the R-squared for each outcome (as opposed to the variance explained by each factor across multiple indicators).

summary(fit, rsq = TRUE)

messages.subject: Re: Explained variance for CFA(?)
messages.subject_clean: Explained variance for CFA(?)
messages.body_plain:
> is there a statistical reason why the cfa() output does not provide Proportion Var or an equivalent?

There is a theoretical reason.   How much variance across indicators that a factor explains was developed as a justification for whether to retain that factor from an EFA.  In CFA, you justification for retaining a factor is the reason that you specified it to begin with:  that is the factor that you meant to measure with the indicators.

> Should we be avoiding attempting this comparison or even obtaining explained variance for CFA at all?

As I said in your second link, you can't clearly delineate "this" from "that" variance being explained by "this" or "that" factor when the factors are correlated.  I think it is already a muddy interpretation in EFA when an oblique rotation is used.

> I have attempted to calculate this value myself through a custom function

Looks nice, I think those are the right formulas.  See also Jeremy's comments in this thread:
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/128671/minimum-cumulative-variance-to-extract-in-exploratory-factor-analysis-to-ensure

> The idea would be to compare two distributions/histograms of 10,000 bootstrapped samples of the explained variances for the EFA and CFA, respectively, to see if they overlap, and to what extent. Would that approach make sense?

I see nothing wrong with that exploration, but what is the purpose?  EFA will explain more variance because it estimates more loadings.  Are you looking for a way to show that adding cross-loadings to a CFA doesn't explain much more variance?  If your goal is to justify being satisfied with the approximate fit of the CFA, I don't think this provides a justification because the EFA and CFA have the same functional forms, but less/more restrictive versions of the same model.  Your model can fail in ways beyond not estimating enough parameters.

> The output, however, provides 275 impossible values (out of 10,000)—i.e., values greater than 1 (the variance explained shouldn't be greater than 1). Would there be any explanation for this?

You are calculating the sum of squared loadings.  That can lead to > 1 when standardized loadings > 1 or (sometimes equivalently) when residual variances < 0, i.e.. Heywood cases, which can occur simply due to sampling error: https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124112442138

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Interpreting and dealing with nonsignificant results of CFA
messages.subject_clean: Interpreting and dealing with nonsignificant results of CFA
messages.body_plain:
> Should the covariances be less than 0.1 to be accepted as satisfactory results?

I have never seen a larger criterion, but I have seen smaller.  Usually people are satisfied when their model-implied (co)variances are within 0.05 or 0.10  SDs of their observed (co)variances.  If your model perfectly reproduces variances (typical when residual variances are unconstrained), it should be equivalent to requesting correlation residuals

lavResiduals(fit, type = "cor")

So you could think perhaps more intuitively about whether your model-implied correlations are within 0.05 or 0.10 of observed correlations.

The point is that mediocre model fit is the accumulation of all the ways your predictions differ from your observations.  Those can include a (few) major misspecification(s), or it could reflect many minor misspecifications.  It is up to you to decide how large of a deviation from observations would be important to address.  The practice of SEM is notorious for lacking objective criteria for making such judgements because they must be based on the substantive domain in which the research is conducted.  There is no magic number that is a good or bad criterion.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
